body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Practice management system prompts and highest-priority critically important antimicrobial use in small-animal clinics: a before-after study","authors":"Lindqvist-Oduya M, Farrant-Achebe J, Tomasz-Reyes K","year":2021,"venue":"Companion Animal Stewardship Journal","doi":"10.5555/casj.2021.0114","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Background: highest-priority critically important antimicrobials (HPCIAs) are often prescribed in companion animal practice without culture. Methods: three first-opinion small-animal clinics added a prompt to their practice management system that appeared whenever an HPCIA was selected and asked for a culture result or a recorded reason. We compared weekly prescribing for 20 weeks before and 20 weeks after the change. Results: the share of systemic antimicrobial prescriptions that were HPCIAs fell from 24 to 13 percent. The share of amoxicillin-clavulanate rose by 4 percentage points. Re-consultation within seven days for the same problem did not change (8.1 against 8.4 percent). Reasons entered in the prompt were often brief, such as owner cannot give tablets. Conclusions: a prescribing prompt was followed by lower HPCIA use without a rise in re-consultation; substitution towards other broad-spectrum drugs should be monitored."},{"title":"Monthly benchmarking feedback on antimicrobial prescribing to veterinary practices: a controlled before-after comparison","authors":"Ashworth-Mensah P, Kowalczyk-Idris H","year":2019,"venue":"Veterinary Prescribing Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We sent monthly feedback letters to 24 companion animal practices showing each practice's share of prescriptions that were highest-priority critically important antimicrobials against the anonymised distribution of all participating practices; 26 practices that did not receive letters served as a comparison group. Over six months the HPCIA share fell by a relative 18 percent in practices receiving feedback and by 3 percent in comparison practices. The fall was larger in practices with a named stewardship lead. Practices chose whether to take part, and those receiving feedback had higher baseline HPCIA use, so part of the fall may be regression to the mean. No clinical outcomes were measured."},{"title":"Stewardship interventions for highest-priority antimicrobials in first-opinion companion animal practice: a systematic review of fourteen evaluations","authors":"Nakagawa-Pryce R, Obuya-Lindberg T, Castell-Moreau A","year":2023,"venue":"Pellmoor Small Animal Quality Reports","doi":"10.5555/sapqr.2023.0207","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched four bibliographic databases and two veterinary conference archives to 2022 for evaluations of stewardship interventions in first-opinion companion animal practice. Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Twelve used before-after designs and two had a concurrent comparison group. Guidelines combined with audit and feedback were followed by lower use of highest-priority critically important antimicrobials in nine of ten studies that measured it; guidelines alone showed little change. Only four studies reported re-consultation or treatment failure, and none reported owner-reported outcomes. Heterogeneous indicators prevented pooling. Most studies were at serious risk of bias from secular trends and from practices choosing to take part."},{"title":"Urine culture before antimicrobial treatment in dogs and cats with lower urinary tract signs: submission rates and culture results in first-opinion practice","authors":"Ferreira-Dunmore L, Haugen-Adeyemi S","year":2020,"venue":"Clinical Urology in Companion Animals","doi":"10.5555/cuca.2020.0056","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed consultations for lower urinary tract signs in 1,240 cats and 860 dogs across eleven first-opinion clinics over two years. A urine culture was submitted for 11 percent of cats and 19 percent of dogs before an antimicrobial was prescribed. Of cats with lower urinary tract signs that had a urine culture, 27 percent grew bacteria, compared with 62 percent of cultured dogs. Most cats whose culture grew nothing had already received an antimicrobial on the day of the consultation. Culture cost was the reason most often recorded when owners declined. The authors suggest that routine culture in cats with lower urinary tract signs could avoid many unnecessary prescriptions."},{"title":"Owner expectations of antimicrobials and satisfaction after companion animal consultations: a questionnaire study","authors":"Whitcombe-Osei D, Marchetti-Lund F","year":2022,"venue":"Companion Animal Stewardship Journal","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked 412 dog and cat owners after first-opinion consultations whether they had expected an antimicrobial and how satisfied they were with the visit. Thirty-eight percent had expected an antimicrobial. Satisfaction was similar among owners who received an antimicrobial and those who did not when the veterinary surgeon explained the diagnosis and gave a recheck plan. Owners who expected an antimicrobial, did not receive one and were given no explanation reported the lowest satisfaction. Owners of cats were more likely than owners of dogs to say that giving tablets at home would be difficult. Responses came from four clinics in one region, and the response rate was 46 percent."},{"title":"Weekly extraction of antimicrobial prescribing indicators from practice management systems: agreement with case-note review","authors":"Dahl-Okafor B, Pennington-Sato M, Iyer-Walsh C","year":2024,"venue":"Clinical Veterinary Audit Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/cvaq.2024.0033","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared antimicrobial prescribing indicators extracted automatically each week from the practice management systems of six small-animal clinics with manual review of the case notes for a random sample of 600 prescriptions. Automated extraction correctly identified the drug class, including highest-priority critically important antimicrobials, for 94 percent of prescriptions. Only 61 percent of prescriptions carried a coded reason, so indicators restricted to a clinical indication, such as suspected urinary infection, needed a free-text search that missed about one case in five. Weekly extraction took about 15 minutes per clinic once the report was built. We recommend drug-class indicators for routine monitoring and periodic manual sampling for indication-specific measures."},{"title":"Why veterinary surgeons choose long-acting cephalosporin injections for cats: a focus group study in first-opinion practice","authors":"Okonjo-Hartley E, Brandvold-Kaur S","year":2018,"venue":"Veterinary Prescribing Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held six focus groups with 31 veterinary surgeons from first-opinion practices to explore why long-acting cephalosporin injections are chosen for cats. Participants described difficulty giving tablets to cats, doubts about whether owners would complete a course, short consultation times and a fear that owners would move to another practice if sent home with tablets. Several said an injection felt kinder to the cat. Participants suggested that a practical handout on giving tablets, a nurse appointment to demonstrate it and a follow-up telephone call would make them more comfortable prescribing oral first-line drugs. Participants were volunteers who may have held stronger views than their colleagues."}]}
